proposal.utterance: What BFO category best fits 'the normative force of an obligation'?

entities.label: NormativeForce
entities.rationale: Normative force is the capacity or power of an obligation to bind, direct, or compel action. It is internally grounded in the obligation (or in the bearer of the obligation) and is not merely a contingent external label. This matches BFO Disposition (BFO_0000016): a realizable entity that is intrinsic to its bearer and is grounded in the physical or social constitution of that bearer. It is distinct from a Role (externally conferred) and from a Quality (a static measurable property). Normative force can be realized in processes of compliance, enforcement, or deliberation, which further supports the Disposition typing.

relations.rationale: NormativeForce is typed as a subclass of Disposition (BFO_0000016) because normative force is an intrinsic, internally grounded capacity of an obligation that can be realized in processes of compliance or enforcement.

Open question alternative — if normative force is treated as a quality/disposition that inheres in a LegalObligation rather than a subclass of it, the relation would instead be RO_0000052 (inheres in) from an instance of NormativeForce to an instance of LegalObligation. This subClassOf assertion should be reviewed against the open question below.

open_questions: Should NormativeForce be modeled as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) inhering in a LegalObligation individual, or as a Quality (BFO_0000019) of the obligation? Disposition is preferred if normative force is a capacity that can be realized in compliance/enforcement processes; Quality is preferred if it is treated as a static, measurable property of the norm.

Is 'normative force' always specifically legal, or should it be a more general class with LegalNormativeForce as a subclass? This affects whether it should inhere in working:LegalObligation specifically or in a broader NormativeObligation class.

Should the subClassOf relation to LegalObligation be removed in favor of an inheres-in restriction (i.e., NormativeForce inheres_in some LegalObligation), which would be more faithful to BFO's treatment of specifically dependent continuants?
proposal.rationale_summary: The normative force of an obligation is best typed as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) in BFO 2020. A Disposition is a specifically dependent continuant that is internally grounded in its bearer — here, the obligation or the agent bearing the obligation — and that can be realized in occurrent processes such as acts of compliance, enforcement proceedings, or deliberative processes. It is not a Quality because normative force is not merely a static measurable attribute but a dynamic capacity. It is not a Role because roles are externally conferred social functions rather than intrinsic capacities. The proposed class NormativeForce is minted as a subclass of BFO_0000016, with a tentative subClassOf link to the existing working:LegalObligation flagged for review, since in strict BFO the preferred modeling would be a universal restriction (NormativeForce inheres_in some LegalObligation) rather than a subClassOf relation between a disposition class and an obligation class.
